name: Arrangement: loop to full song in 8-bar blocks (intro, build, drop, breakdown, outro)
goal: Turn a loop into a finished electronic/pop arrangement: start from the full loop (the climax), subtract to make sections, change something every 8 bars, build-ups with risers and snare rolls, pre-drop low-end removal, breakdowns, withheld reveals and rule-of-three phrasing.

theory: Energy curve: listeners need contrast; repetition builds expectation, change rewards it. Sections are 8/16 bars; a one-beat gap or bass removal before the drop maximizes impact.
prerequisites: A DAW arrangement with gain automation and markers
A DAW or step sequencer with drum or percussion voices
A DAW project with the track's intro/breakdown and drop already laid out
A DAW with arrangement view, markers and filter automation
A DAW with duplicate-time, insert-time and split commands
A controller or automation for performing one element (optional)
A filter on the pad and bass, one tom or short-fill sample, optional short sweep
A finished 8-16 bar loop (drums, bass, chords, lead, atmosphere)
A finished drop (chords + melody) in a DAW
A finished loop (16 bars in the video)
A loop with an ostinato/arp, bass, pad, percussion and a lead
A loop-based arrangement with kick, closed and open hat loops, clap, bass, pad and a simple lead

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: Rendered part or recipe following the workflow

constraints: Portable recipe; not affiliated with any vendor; do not copy factory presets or sample packs.
Numbers in variants come from the source video transcripts; workflow steps are the consolidated mainstream practice.
Bring drums in early and avoid pitch wobble unless asked (user preferences from daily tests).

steps.action: Build the full 8-bar loop first (the drop/climax), then copy it across the timeline and subtract elements to create earlier sections.
Map the energy curve on a reference track: intro 16-32, build 8, drop 16-32, breakdown 16, build 8, drop 2, outro mirrors intro.
Every 8 bars add or remove at least one element; intro: high-passed kick, filtered bass, root pedal before the progression.
Build: 7 bars of risers and snare roll doubling (4->8->16), last bar remove low end / kick, double kick or vocal pickup.
Drop on the one with impact; breakdown strips rhythm and foreshadows melody through a low-pass.
Rule of three: play an idea twice, third time change it; withhold one key element (bass motion, melody) until the climax.
Transitions without risers: solo the lead, filter pad down, drop kick for a bar, single tom hit.
Outro mirrors the intro for DJ-friendly mixing.
Hear the theory: run `/home/box/audio-tools/bin/python sample-lab/theory/arrangement_energy.py` from the repo root and compare the sections; reuse its functions as a starting point for renders.
steps.expect: WAV in sample-lab/theory/out/ demonstrating the principle

verification: Render a short test and A/B against a reference at matched loudness
Run the generator and confirm it writes a WAV without error
Check mono compatibility and that no element masks the kick/bass

variants.name: Breakdown arrangement after a drop: 4-bar break of impacts and reverse sweeps, two 8-bar breakdown halves (chords from the drop with rhythm removed, melody simplified then foreshadowed through a rising lowpass), then an 8-bar build-up of chopped parts and one silent bar before the drop
variants.goal: Lay out the section after a drop with markers: Break (4 bars) → Breakdown 1 (8) → Breakdown 2 (8) → Build-up (8) → drop. Break: big impact, sub drop, reverse crashes/sweeps and a quiet ambience bed. Breakdown effects first: repeat impacts and sub drops at each breakdown start, add a quiet background-motion loop and shaker with lots of reverb and low dry level. Breakdown harmony: copy the chords from the drop, remove the rhythm and merge notes into long chords, and simplify offbeat notes. Layer a soft piano with a second synth, and add automation (volume or cutoff rising at the end of each repetition) for reverse-like tension; make a reverse piano by recording a hit and reversing it. Melody: use the drop melody simplified (first four notes, rest, next five). Breakdown 2: same material plus 'drop clap' accents with reverb to signal the second half, a simple piano melody, and the full drop melody low-pass filtered in with an automation ramp from closed to open. Build-up: chop breakdown sounds down to the first chord repeated, chop more in the second half, add up-filters, reverse sweeps/impacts at the start, a snare fill (4 hits then doubled), melody foreshadowed with its ending in the last bar, then everything cut one bar before the drop.
steps: Place markers: Break (4 bars), Breakdown 1 (8), Breakdown 2 (8), Build-up (8), then the drop returns.
Break: big impact, sub drop, reverse crashes, a reversed sweep going up, plus a background ambience effect.
Breakdown background: repeat impacts and sub drops at the start of each breakdown, add smaller impacts, a motion loop and a shaker with reverb and reduced dry level.

Chords: copy the drop chords, delete rhythm so notes become long chords (Ctrl+L to legato-join), remove offbeat notes, play on soft piano layered with a second synth; keep within one scale using scale highlighting.
Tension motion: automate the synth's volume or cutoff rising at the end of each repetition; make a reverse piano by recording a piano hit and reversing it, then place it in the gap.

Melody: take the first four notes of the drop melody, leave space, then the next five; for Breakdown 2 add drop-claps with reverb, a simple piano melody, and the full drop melody low-passed with an automation ramp from fully closed to open.

Build-up: chop breakdown sounds to the first chord repeated, chop more in the second half, add up-filters, reverse sweeps and impacts at the start, a snare fill (four hits then doubled), keep the drop claps, bring in the real melody gradually filtered, put the melody ending in the last bar, and turn everything off one bar before the drop.

variants.name: Eight-bar build-up template: seven bars of risers, drums and sustained parts, one bar of pre-drop with everything cut, low end automated away, kick doubling schedule, filtered-in snare, single-note pad with pitch rise, and a readable vocal before the drop
variants.goal: Build a 4/4 build-up before a drop. Structure: 8 bars (16 bars for drum and bass). Seven bars of risers, drums and sustained instruments; the final bar is the pre-drop where everything else cuts off (snare roll, pre-drop vocal, sub build). Transitions: into the build-up use quiet up-risers and down-filters starting at its first bar; take one note of a chord-progression pad, hold it for the build, and automate pitch up over the last four bars; use vocals that actually say something in the last four bars (chop only the first four); thin the drums before the build if there is no breakdown, filter them in gradually if there is. Into the drop: always include one pre-drop bar, gradually automate low end out of bass, pads and risers, and optionally dip the loudest elements (not vocals) just before the drop. Elements: kick every beat for 4 bars, doubled for 2, doubled again for 1 (and through the last bar if the vocal matches), filtering out as it goes; a snare every step, filtering in from already half-open, plus a second low snare after 4 bars; hats/claps/percussion loop for depth; bring back an element from the intro/breakdown as a sustained part with a riser; layer multiple quiet risers.
steps: Set the length: 8 bars for 4/4 styles, 16 bars for faster drum and bass. Typical layout: 16-bar intro, optional 8-bar breakdown, 8-bar build-up, drop.

Bars 1-7: risers, drums and sustained instruments; bar 8: pre-drop where everything else cuts off (snare roll, pre-drop vocal, sub build). Do not skip the pre-drop bar unless the groove rolls straight into the drop.
Start quiet up-risers and down-filters at bar 1 of the build-up so the transition into it carries momentum; layer several risers, all low in level.
Take one note of the previous chord pad, hold it for the whole build-up, keep it static for four bars, then automate pitch rising over the last four bars.
Vocals: chop them in the first four bars; make the last four bars (pre-drop) say something recognisable. If a full vocal runs through the track, skip chops.

Drums: with no breakdown, remove some drums in the transition so the return hits harder; with a breakdown, filter elements in gradually instead. Kick: every beat for 4 bars, double time for 2 bars, double again for 1 bar (continue through the pre-drop bar if the vocal matches), filtering out as it goes.
Snare: a hit every step, filtered in starting already half-open; after 4 bars add a second low snare; add hats, claps and a percussion loop for movement. Stop all drums at the pre-drop.

Remove low end as you approach the drop: automate bass, pads and risers' low frequencies down gradually. Optionally dip the loudest non-vocal elements (instruments/drums) rather than the master if vocals are present.

variants.name: Eight-bar rhythmic phrasing: spine beat on strong beats, bar-level A/B/A/C variation, and a last-bar D that is either a fill (adds syncopation and toms) or an empty (drops the kick or main rhythm) to set up the next section
variants.goal: Turn a one-bar loop into an 8-bar phrase that tells the listener where the section boundaries are. Build a spine beat (kick on 1-2-3-4, snare/clap on the backbeat 2 and 4, closed hat on the offbeat 'ands'), then put lighter percussion on the weak 16ths ('e' and 'a'), mixing low-mid and high sounds there. Use bar-level variation: A = core bar, B = one small change (add, remove or swap one hit), back to A in bar 3, C = a slightly bigger change at bar 4, then A material again, and D in bar 8: either a fill (extra syncopation, snare hits on weak beats, extra eighth-note kicks, toms high to low) or an empty (remove most or all main rhythmic elements, e.g. drop the kick for the last bar) before the next downbeat. The bigger the coming change, the more anticipation the fill or empty should build. Optionally layer a polymeter (for example a 3-step pattern over a 4-beat grid) so loops shift against each other over time.
steps: Build the spine beat: kick on beats 1-4, snare or clap on 2 and 4, closed hat on each offbeat eighth ('and').
Add ghost or weak-beat hits on the 'e' and 'a' 16ths with quieter or lighter sounds (ghost snares, percussion, toms, synth hits), mixing low-mid and high-frequency sounds.
Set the bar to A. Make bar 2 B: one small change only (add, remove or swap one hit). Bar 3 returns to A.
Make bar 4 C: a slightly bigger variation than B (it doesn't need to include B's change). This closes the 4-bar half-phrase.
Bars 5-7: return to A material (optionally a light B variant).

Bar 8 = D. If the next section is a big lift, write a fill: extra syncopation, snares on weak beats, a couple of extra eighth-note kicks, toms stepping high to low. If you want a vacuum instead, write an empty: remove most or all main elements, e.g. drop the kick for the whole bar (or just its last beat).
Line up section changes with the downbeat after D, and repeat the 8-bar scheme for every section, choosing fill or empty each time.
Optional: add a polymeter layer (a 3-step pattern on the same grid as 4-beat bars) so its accent drifts against the downbeat.

variants.name: Four levels of loop-to-story arrangement: (1) subtractive Lego-block arrangement from a duplicated loop shaped by an energy contour, (2) turnaround-and-marker transitions at section edges, (3) a performed protagonist element that crescendos and decrescendos across sections, (4) an additive cinematic pass that starts from silence and adds only motivated elements
variants.goal: Turn a 16-bar loop into a musical story in four escalating levels. Level 1 (subtractive): duplicate the loop across the whole target length (4-5 minutes), then cut away in 8- or 16-bar blocks following an energy contour (low start, build to the middle, kick-out dips, peak, outro); add a little silence at the start and room at the end for reverb tails. Level 2 (transitions): at each section edge add a turnaround (signals the end: remove low energy, reverse reverb swell or noise riser) and a marker on the downbeat (a splash: white noise, crash, one percussion hit into big reverb, stutter or false drop), built from the track's own timbres resampled, reversed or processed; transitions can be explicit or hypnotic. Level 3 (performance): record a performed element (e.g. filter, level or intensity moves on one sound) that starts mellow, grows to dominant and subsides, spanning section boundaries as the 'protagonist'; split and move the audio if needed. Level 4 (additive): start from silence and add elements only when the music is motivated (when you would get bored), like a film composer, letting well-designed elements play for a long time.
steps: Decide the target length; select the loop and duplicate it end to end until the timeline exceeds that length; trim any extra.

Sketch an energy contour: low start, additions toward the middle, dips where the kick goes away, a maximum, then an outro. Optionally align a reference track to the grid and copy its arrangement (not its sounds).
Subtract in 8- or 16-bar blocks so each section boundary adds some elements and removes others. Insert a little silence at the start and leave space at the end for reverb tails.
At each section edge, add a turnaround in the last bar(s): remove low-end energy and add a reverse reverb swell or noise riser built from the track's own sounds.
On the new section's downbeat, add a marker: white noise burst, crash, one percussion hit into a big reverb, a stutter, or a false drop (withhold the first hit).
Revisit breaks and drops: e.g. a very sparse moment, then build, build, build, then a short silence before the drop.

Pick one protagonist element and perform it across the whole track (record filter/level/intensity moves) so it starts mellow, grows dominant and subsides, crossing section boundaries; split and rearrange the performance if needed.
Additive pass: from silence, peel everything back to almost nothing and add elements one at a time only when the music needs them (when you notice boredom), giving each element time and space.

variants.name: Loop-to-track arrangement where the finished loop is the climax and everything before it 'gives away' that loop gradually: whole elements, the power of elements (high-passed kick, thin high-and-low-passed bass), and the chord progression itself (root-note pedal first), with a change at every 8-bar boundary and an outro that mirrors the intro
variants.goal: Arrange a finished loop into a full track. First map a reference track: listen through and drop markers for what enters or leaves at each section (every 8 bars something changes). Treat your loop as the climax and plan how to reach it by giving things away over time. Drums first: copy the full drum loop to the start, high-pass the kick at about 120 Hz for the first 16 bars, start with fewer parts (no shaker/hats), bring shaker in, save hats and snare for later, and remove the kick's last bar (or last two bars) before each full-kick entry or drop. Atmosphere runs throughout. Bass: start as a single root-note pedal (monotonic) instead of the progression, with an octave jump at the end of each 8 bars; give away its power with labelled high-pass and low-pass filters automated from thin and dark to full. Melodic parts: bring in stripped-back fragments (first bar only, fewer notes), filter elements in instead of hard entries, reveal the full chord progression and full lead later; hold back some parts for the second drop. Outro: do the opposite of the intro (high-pass the kick again for 8 bars, filter the bass out and darker, return to the root pedal and a resolving last note).
steps: Import a reference track, listen through and drop a marker each time something enters, leaves or changes (expect a change every 8 bars). Write the macro structure, e.g. intro, bass in, build, drop, breakdown, drop 2, outro.
List what you can give away: whole elements; element power (kick without lows, bass without sub, thinner versions); the chord progression; stripped-back versions of parts.

Drums first: copy the full drum loop to the start; high-pass the kick at about 120 Hz for the first 16 bars; remove shaker, hats and snare at first and stage them in later (shaker early, hats and snare saved for later).
Delete the kick's last bar (or last 2 bars) before each full-kick entry or drop.
Run the atmosphere/texture throughout to set the tone.

Bass: write a single root-note pedal for the early sections with an octave jump at the end of each 8 bars. Add labelled HP and LP filters and automate from thin and dark to full and bright; switch to the full chord progression only at the main section.

Melodic parts: enter with fragments (first bar only, fewer notes), filter them in rather than hard-cutting, then reveal the full progression, full lead and extra layers (piano chords, high pluck) only at later peaks; hold some back for drop 2.
Before a drop, filter percussion/kick from thin and clicky to full, leave a short moment of near-silence, then hit the drop with everything un-high-passed.
Outro: mirror the intro: high-pass the kick for 8 bars, filter the bass out and darker, return to the root pedal and end on a resolving note.

variants.name: Rule of three for repeating musical ideas: play a 4-bar idea twice so it sticks, then on the third pass either go somewhere new (new melody on the same chords, or new chords) or start the same and diverge halfway
variants.goal: Stop over-looping a phrase. Play a musical idea (e.g. a 4-bar chord progression with melody) once to spark interest and a second time to reinforce it so the listener can remember it. On the third pass, never repeat it unchanged: option 1, go somewhere different (a new melody over the same chords, or a new progression with a new melody); option 2, start the third pass the same and diverge partway (around halfway through the phrase). Choose the option by intent (the response you want from the listener). Use as a check across a loop-based arrangement.
steps: Write or pick a 4-bar idea (progression + melody) and place it once.
Repeat it once (2 passes in total) so it is reinforced and memorable.
Third pass, option 1: go somewhere different: keep the chords and write a new melody, or move to a new progression with a new melody.
Third pass, option 2: start identical to the first two passes, then change the melody or chords about halfway through the phrase.
Choose option 1 or 2 by the section's intent and audit the whole arrangement: anywhere an idea plays 3+ times unchanged, apply one of the two options.

variants.name: Three section transitions with no big risers or snare rolls, for simple two-chord tracks: (1) the lead plays alone while the pad's filter closes, a simple sweep and a lead variation, then kick, hats and bass drop in; (2) keep open hats, filter the pad down, put a clap on the beat with no kick and a high-passed bass, loop a lead variation, then one quarter-note tom hit opens the drop with the bass filter removed; (3) strip to the hat loop, tease lead variations (velocity, pan, spacing) with no kick or bass, then a very short fill and everything returns at once
variants.goal: Make transitions by subtraction and re-entry instead of piling on FX. Simple material needs simple transitions. The kick-plus-bass re-entry is the payoff, and the kick acts as the track's metronome that listeners wait for. A riser-free counterpart to the section transition toolkit and the three-track automation sketch.
steps: Intro to first drop: run the intro with just the kick and a closed-hat drum loop, and the pad opening and closing on a filter. At the end, let the pluck/lead play on its own with the pad filter coming down, a simple sweep and a lead variation as the last bar.
Land the first drop with kick, closed hats, open hats and the bassline entering together.

Mid transition, part 1: play a lead variation, then return to the original. Keep the open hats, low-pass the pad steadily down, mute kick and closed hats, add a clap on the beat and high-pass the bassline.
Mid transition, part 2: loop the lead variation and let the clap settle. Place one tom hit (about a quarter note long) in the last beat's space before the downbeat.
Re-enter all drums with the second lead variation, open hats and the bass with its filter removed, so the low end hits with the kick.

Final payoff: strip back to the closed-hat loop and open hats with the pad dipping again, with no kick and no bass. Tease the lead with its variations (same notes, different velocity, pan and spacing, for example one extra bar of space).
End the tease with a very short drum fill (sweep plus clap/snare), then bring everything back at once: drums, bass, pad and lead.

variants.name: Arrangement that saves several 'firsts' for one climactic moment: keep a three-note ostinato unchanged from the start to that moment, keep the bass on one note until then, and change the ostinato, start the moving bassline and bring in a new percussion layer and the lead together; pull the constant pad from about -3 dB to about -14 dB in full sections, mark every entry or exit with a small FX hit, put a short silence before big mutes, and keep intro and outro loopable
variants.goal: Delta vs the existing loop-is-the-climax and four-levels arrangement skills: those reveal the loop gradually; this one holds one element deliberately unchanged and stacks several first-time changes into one moment. Structure from the video: loopable intro (no fade noise across the loop point); the arpeggio/ostinato and a filtered kick from the start; a feedback drone building; around 1 minute in, bassline, snare and the rest come together; take your time with the build-up but not 2 minutes; a short break optional; faster hats and opening the arp filter for an early peak; low-cut the bass to put focus on the arp. In the drop keep the bass on one note. In full sections check each channel and mute what is not needed; turn the constant pad down from about -3 dB to about -14 dB. Mark each entry or exit with small FX or drum fills (orchestral hits in the intro). After about 3.5-4 minutes, change the arp for the first time at the same moment the moving bassline enters, a new off-beat shaker enters, the lead enters and the pad plays the arp's harmony. Then the drop: the bass stops briefly while the hats keep running; every 8 bars switch one element. Put a quick moment of silence before muting many channels. Build down slowly and keep the outro loopable but not overly long for album versions.
steps: Make the intro loopable: no fade-in noise or tails across the loop point so it can be repeated or mixed.
Start the ostinato and a filtered kick from the beginning; add a building drone; bring in bassline, snare and other drums around the 1-minute mark (build-up shorter than about 2 minutes).
Write the held-back list: ostinato change, moving bassline, a new percussion layer (e.g. off-beat shaker), the lead, pad switching to the ostinato's harmony.
In the drops before the reveal, keep the bass on one note and low-cut it at times so focus stays on the ostinato.
In full sections solo-check each channel and mute anything not needed; automate the constant pad from about -3 dB down to about -14 dB.
Mark every entry or exit with a small FX hit, drum fill or (in the intro) an orchestral hit.
Before muting many channels at once, insert a short moment of silence.
At the reveal point change the ostinato for the first time, start the moving bassline, add the new percussion layer and the lead, and move the pad to the ostinato's harmony, all on the same downbeat.
In the following drop let the bass stop briefly while hats keep running; then switch one element every 8 bars (add, remove, or octave shift).
Build down slowly to a loopable outro; keep it shorter for album versions.
